title: The tie at the far side

data.source: Jacobi (1837), Poincare (1905), Morse (1934), Bott (1956), Milnor (1963); cited from memory. Computed from the eigenvalues of exact matrices.

prediction: On a sphere the index of a great-circle path jumps from 0 to 1 at the antipode; on the intrinsic circle the index is 0 at every length and nothing changes in the second variation at the half-turn. The half-turn there is a tie between two equally short ways round, not an instability.
baseline: Morse's index theorem (1934), conjugate points (Jacobi 1837) and the cut locus (Poincare 1905); Milnor (1963). Decoy: index = number of half-turns completed.
relation: identical to the cut point of a circle in Poincare's sense; not a conjugate point
claim_posed_by: this room; Phoenix does not make it
status_line: CRR here is: a renaming of the cut point of a circle (a tie between two equally short ways round); Morse theory finds no instability there, unlike the antipode of a sphere.
why: On a sphere a path that passes the antipode can be shortened by pushing it sideways: the index jumps, and the antipode is both conjugate point and cut point. On the intrinsic circle that R1 chooses (Phoenix status ASSUMPTION) there is no sideways. The index stayed 0 at every length and the second variation did not notice the half-turn. What happens at a is only that the other way round becomes as short. So the place R2 (ASSUMPTION) cuts at is Poincare's cut point of the 'second geodesic' kind. The claim of instability is one this room posed, and it does not hold; Phoenix does not make it.
